chapters.name: Chapter 1: A healthy pregnancy and a safe birth

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Clinic visits during pregnancy
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a plan of clinic visits for a pregnancy, starting in the first 12 weeks.
This lesson builds toward: Given a pregnancy in your family and its due month, you will write a clinic visit plan for the pregnancy that starts in the first 12 weeks, with at least eight contacts as WHO advises, or the number your clinic gives you.
Care during pregnancy is called antenatal care. At each visit, the nurse or midwife checks the mother's blood pressure, weight and blood, listens to the baby, and gives the care your country's clinic offers. Many problems can be found early, before they become dangerous.
WHO advises at least eight contacts with a health worker during pregnancy, and the first one in the first 12 weeks (the first three months). So as soon as a woman thinks she is pregnant, she goes to the clinic. Your clinic may give you its own schedule; follow it.
At the first visit, the clinic usually gives a mother-and-child health booklet or card. The name differs by country (for example, Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook or Ghana's Maternal and Child Health Record Book). Keep it in a plastic bag, bring it to every visit, and write the next date on your phone calendar.
Fathers and family help too: help with transport money, go to a visit with her, and let her rest. Ask the clinic or your health insurance office whether pregnancy care is free or covered where you live; this changes, so ask each time.
Step by step:
- Go to the clinic as soon as you think you are pregnant, ideally in the first 12 weeks.
- Ask how many visits the clinic plans and when.
- Write each date in the booklet and on your phone calendar.
- Bring the booklet to every visit.
- If you miss a visit, go as soon as you can; do not wait for the next one.
Words to know:
- Antenatal care: health checks for a woman during pregnancy, before the baby is born.
- Contact: a visit or meeting with a health worker, at the clinic or at home.
- Midwife: a trained health worker who cares for women in pregnancy, birth and after birth.
Official sources:
- WHO: New guidelines on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience (eight contacts, first in the first 12 weeks)
Try it now: Take a pregnancy in your family, or the example of Fatou in Thiès, Senegal, who is 10 weeks pregnant. Write the month of the first visit and list the months of the next visits. Next to each, write who will go with her.
You can now plan clinic visits for a pregnancy, starting early, and keep the dates where you will see them.

check.q: When should a woman make her first clinic visit in pregnancy?
options: Only when the baby is about to come
As soon as she thinks she is pregnant, ideally in the first 12 weeks
check.why: WHO advises the first contact in the first 12 weeks, so problems are found early.

check.q: How many contacts with a health worker does WHO advise during pregnancy?
check.why: WHO advises at least eight contacts; your clinic may give its own schedule.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Danger signs in pregnancy and after birth
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the danger signs that mean a pregnant woman or new mother must go to the clinic now.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of signs during pregnancy or after birth, you will pick out the danger signs that mean the woman must go to the clinic now, getting at least 4 of 5 right and choosing "go now" instead of "wait and see".
Most pregnancies go well. But some signs mean danger for the mother or the baby. With these signs, do not wait to see if they pass, and do not wait for the next visit. Go to the clinic or hospital now, day or night.
Danger signs in pregnancy: bleeding from the vagina; a bad headache with blurred vision; fits (convulsions); swelling of the face and hands; fever; strong pain in the belly; the baby moving much less or not at all; water breaking before labour; trouble breathing.
Danger signs after birth: heavy bleeding (soaking cloths or pads quickly); fever; bad-smelling discharge; a bad headache, blurred vision or fits; pain or swelling in one leg; feeling very sad or unable to cope for many days.
Heavy bleeding, infection and high blood pressure are among the main causes of death in pregnancy and birth, and they can kill fast. Speed saves lives. Call the community health worker or the emergency number your area uses on the way.
Step by step:
- Learn the danger signs and stick the list on the wall at home.
- If you see one, stop what you are doing.
- Go to the clinic or hospital now with the booklet.
- Call ahead or call the community health worker on the way.
Words to know:
- Danger sign: a sign that the mother or baby may be in serious danger and needs care now.
- Convulsions (fits): sudden shaking of the body that the person cannot control.
- Discharge: fluid that comes out of the vagina.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Maternal mortality (main causes; skilled care before, during and after birth)
Try it now: Write the danger signs for pregnancy and after birth on one sheet, in your own language if you prefer. Add the name of the nearest clinic and an emergency phone number. Put it on the wall or save a photo on your phone.
You can now pick out the danger signs in pregnancy and after birth and know to go to the clinic at once.

check.q: Mariam in Bouaké is 7 months pregnant and has a bad headache and blurred vision. What should she do?
options: Rest and see how she feels tomorrow
Wait for her next clinic visit
Drink more water and lie down
Go to the clinic or hospital now
check.why: A bad headache with blurred vision is a danger sign; it can mean dangerously high blood pressure.

check.q: Which is a danger sign after birth?
options: Heavy bleeding that soaks cloths quickly
Wanting to sleep when the baby sleeps
check.why: Heavy bleeding after birth is a main cause of death in mothers and needs care now.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making a birth plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a birth plan that names the place, the transport, the money and the helpers.
This lesson builds toward: For a coming birth, you will write a birth plan naming the health facility, the transport, the money put aside and the people who will help, with every part filled in and agreed with the family before the last month.
Many dangers in birth happen fast and are hard to see coming. Care from a skilled health worker (a midwife, nurse or doctor) during and after birth saves the lives of mothers and babies. So the safest plan is to give birth at a health facility.
A birth plan answers simple questions before labour starts: Which health facility? How will we get there at night? Who will pay for the transport, and how much have we put aside? Who goes with her? Who minds the other children? Who could give blood if needed?
Start saving early, a little each week. For example, a family in Kisumu puts aside KES 200 a week, and a family in Tamale puts aside GHS 20 a week (these are example amounts; plan your own). Save the boda boda, okada, taxi or ambulance number in the phone now.
Pack a small bag in the last months: the health booklet, clean cloths, clothes and a cap for the baby, and things for the mother. Agree the plan with the whole family so nobody argues when labour begins.
Step by step:
- Choose the health facility and visit it before the birth if you can.
- Arrange transport for day and night, and save the numbers.
- Save money each week for transport and costs.
- Choose who goes with her and who minds the home.
- Pack the bag and agree the plan with the family.
Words to know:
- Birth plan: a written plan of where and how the baby will be born and how you will get there.
- Skilled health worker: a midwife, nurse or doctor trained to care for births.
- Labour: the pains and work of the body that push the baby out.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Maternal mortality (main causes; skilled care before, during and after birth)
Try it now: Write a birth plan for a pregnancy in your family, or for Amina in Kano who is due in three months. Fill in: facility, transport (day and night), weekly savings, who goes with her, who minds the home, and what is in the bag.
You can now write a birth plan that names the place, the transport, the money and the helpers.

check.q: What is the safest place to give birth?
options: At home with no one trained
A health facility with a skilled health worker
On the way, to save time
check.why: Skilled care during and after birth saves the lives of mothers and newborns.

check.q: When should the family agree the birth plan?
options: Before the last month of pregnancy
Only if there is a problem
check.why: Planning ahead stops delays and arguments when labour starts.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Your baby's first days and first years

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Caring for a newborn in the first days
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the newborn care steps for the first day: warmth, early breastfeeding and a clean cord.
This lesson builds toward: For a baby's first day, you will list the newborn care steps: keep the baby warm, breastfeed within the first hour and keep the cord clean and dry, in the right order and without harmful practices.
A newborn cannot keep itself warm. Dry the baby, then put the baby skin-to-skin on the mother's chest with a cloth over both, and put a cap on. Delay the first bath; ask the health worker when.
Start breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. The first thick, yellow milk (colostrum) is good for the baby; do not throw it away. WHO advises only breast milk for the first 6 months: no water, no tea, no glucose water and no other drinks or foods.
Keep the cord clean and dry. Do not put anything on it unless the health worker tells you to, and wash your hands before touching it. Wash hands with soap before feeding and after changing the baby.
If you can, stay at the facility for about a day after birth, and go to the check-ups after birth that the clinic plans, for both mother and baby. Register the birth and start the vaccines given at birth.
Step by step:
- Dry the baby and put the baby skin-to-skin on the mother, covered, with a cap.
- Breastfeed within the first hour.
- Give only breast milk.
- Keep the cord clean and dry; wash hands before touching it.
- Go to the after-birth check-ups; register the birth; start the vaccines.
Words to know:
- Newborn: a baby in its first 28 days.
- Skin-to-skin: holding the naked baby against the mother's bare chest to keep the baby warm.
- Colostrum: the first thick, yellow breast milk, full of protection for the baby.
- Cord: the part of the umbilical cord still on the baby's belly after birth.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Newborn mortality (newborn care and newborn danger signs)
- WHO fact sheet: Infant and young child feeding
Try it now: Write the newborn care steps for the first day in order, as a short list you could give to a new mother or a grandmother. Then write one harmful habit you have heard of in your area and the safe step that replaces it.
You can now list the newborn care steps for the first day: warmth, early breastfeeding, only breast milk and a clean cord.

options: Within the first hour after birth
check.why: WHO advises starting within the first hour; the first milk protects the baby.

check.q: A relative says to give the newborn water because it is hot. What does WHO advise?
options: Only breast milk for the first 6 months
check.why: Breast milk has all the water a baby under 6 months needs; other drinks can carry germs.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Danger signs in babies and young children
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the danger signs that mean a baby or young child must go to the clinic now.
This lesson builds toward: Given a description of a sick baby or young child, you will identify the danger signs that mean the child must go to the clinic now, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Babies and young children can get very sick very fast. Some signs mean go to the clinic now, not tomorrow.
In a newborn: not feeding well or not able to suck; less active or floppy; fast or difficult breathing; fever, or feeling cold; fits.
In a young child: cannot drink or breastfeed; vomits everything; fits; very sleepy or hard to wake; fast or difficult breathing; fever (in a malaria area, test the same day); diarrhoea with blood, or with sunken eyes and a very thirsty or very weak child.
With diarrhoea, keep breastfeeding and giving drinks and food, and ask the health worker about oral rehydration solution (ORS) and zinc. But if you see a danger sign, go now. Do not use medicines from the market or a neighbour without a health worker's advice.
Step by step:
- Look for the danger signs, even at night.
- If you see one, go to the clinic now with the child health card.
- Keep breastfeeding and giving drinks on the way.
- Call the community health worker if you cannot get there.
Words to know:
- Fits (convulsions): sudden shaking the child cannot control.
- Dehydration: when the body loses too much water, for example through diarrhoea or vomiting.
- ORS: oral rehydration solution: a drink of clean water, salt and sugar that replaces water lost through diarrhoea.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Newborn mortality (newborn care and newborn danger signs)
- WHO fact sheet: Diarrhoeal disease (prevention, home care, signs of dehydration)
Try it now: Make a danger-sign card for babies and young children: one column for newborns, one for older babies and children. Add the nearest clinic, the community health worker's number and how you would get there at night.
You can now spot the danger signs in a baby or young child and get the child to the clinic at once.

check.q: A 3-week-old baby in Kumasi stops sucking and feels cold. What should the family do?
options: Give a medicine from the market
check.why: Not feeding and feeling cold are newborn danger signs that need care now.

check.q: A 2-year-old with diarrhoea has sunken eyes and is very weak. What is right?
check.why: Sunken eyes and weakness are signs of dehydration, which can kill a child; go now.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Feeding, vaccines and growth checks
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find the next vaccine and growth-check dates on the child health card and write the feeding step for the child's age.
This lesson builds toward: Using a child's health card or booklet, you will find the next vaccine and growth-check dates and write the feeding step for the child's age, with no missed visit left unplanned.
The child health card or booklet shows the vaccines given, the next vaccine dates and the growth chart. Vaccines protect against diseases such as measles, polio, whooping cough, tetanus and some kinds of pneumonia and diarrhoea. The schedule differs by country; follow your card and your clinic.
Growth checks at the clinic or with the community health worker weigh and measure the child. A growth line that goes flat or down is a warning: ask the health worker what to do.
Feeding by age (WHO): only breast milk for the first 6 months. From about 6 months, add soft, mashed family foods and keep breastfeeding to 2 years or longer. Start with small amounts and slowly give more, thicker food and more kinds. Babies of 6 to 8 months need 2 to 3 meals a day; children of 9 to 23 months need 3 to 4 meals, with 1 to 2 snacks if needed.
If you miss a vaccine date, do not give up: go as soon as you can and the clinic will catch the child up. Write every next date on your phone calendar.
Step by step:
- Open the child health card.
- Find the last vaccine and the next date.
- Find the last growth check and see if the line is going up.
- Write the feeding step for the child's age.
- Put the next dates on your phone calendar.
Words to know:
- Vaccine: medicine given to protect a child from a disease before they catch it; the clinic gives it on a schedule.
- Growth chart: a chart on the card that shows the child's weight over time.
- Complementary feeding: adding family foods from about 6 months while breastfeeding continues.
Official sources:
- WHO fact sheet: Immunization coverage (what childhood vaccines prevent)
- WHO fact sheet: Infant and young child feeding
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page family health plan. Include the clinic visits still to come, the birth plan, the first-day newborn steps, the danger signs for mother and child with the clinic and an emergency number, and the next vaccine and growth-check dates from the card with the feeding step for the child's age.
You can now read a child health card for the next vaccine and growth-check dates and plan feeding for the child's age.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clinic visits No visit dates, or the first visit is late in pregnancy. Lists the visits still to come, with the first in the first 12 weeks, written in the booklet or on the phone. Also says who goes with her to each visit and how it is paid for. Birth plan One or more of place, transport, money or helpers is missing. Names the facility, day and night transport, weekly savings, who goes with her and who minds the home. Also has transport numbers saved, the bag packed and the plan agreed with the family. Newborn first day Steps are missing, out of order or include a harmful practice. Warmth (skin-to-skin), breastfeeding in the first hour, only breast milk and a clean, dry cord. Also names a local harmful habit and the safe step that replaces it. Danger signs The list misses key signs or says to wait and see. Lists the main danger signs for mother and child, with the nearest clinic and an emergency number. Also covers night-time transport and the community health worker's number. Child danger signs Child danger signs are missing or mixed up with normal signs. Lists the newborn and young child danger signs that mean go now. Explains them clearly enough for a grandmother or older sibling to use. Card, vaccines and feeding No next dates, or feeding advice does not fit the child's age. Gives the next vaccine and growth-check dates from the card and the right feeding step for the age. Dates are on the phone calendar with reminders. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Baby Kofi missed his vaccine date last week. What should the family do?
options: Start again from the first vaccine
Go to the clinic as soon as possible to catch up
check.why: The clinic can catch a child up; go as soon as you can.

check.q: At about what age does a baby start eating family foods as well as breast milk?
check.why: WHO advises adding soft family foods from about 6 months while breastfeeding continues.
